title: Four Sources of Fear
paragraphs: A youth with the resolve to converse only in chaste Tamiḻ, adhering to the tenets of literature and grammar, confided to an elderly person of his hamlet possessing profound knowledge of Tamiḻ, that he would very soon tie the knots. The person greeted him with a heartfelt wish, “May you get an aṇaṅku most suited to your life!”

Incidentally, the youth had browsed the dictionary just that day and found out that aṇaṅku meant ghost. “Sir, why do you wish me to be tied up with a ghost?” The learned elder explained, “Don’t you know that the dictionary details aṇaṅku as ‘a woman’, ‘a ghost’ and a ‘mohini’ (a devil in the guise of a beautiful woman)?” Even in this hi-tech era, there are people horrified by such things as ghost, apparition and black magic. Therefore, in Tolkāppiyam, aṇaṅku is shown as a being evoking fear.

Owing to the fear of lion, tiger, bear and other dangerous animals and being unequal to them in strength and valour, the primitive man hunted them with arrows and spears, while his modern counterpart uses bullets. Of course, they do so from a safe distance.
Laymen as well as the learned are naturally subjected to fear on either hearing about or encountering thieves, groups of robbers or highwaymen.

In this list of things evoking fear, wrong deeds of a serious nature are also included. Many commentators state that iṟai refers to the king. If iṟai is not taken in isolation and read together with the prefix as tam iṟai it becomes tammiṟai, which means ‘one’s wrong deeds of a grievous nature’. It is quite natural that such wrong-doers dread punishment Veḷḷaivāraṇar also points to the double entendre involved in tam iṟai and tammiṟai.
> The four sources of unmitigated fear are > Demoniac beings, wild animals, thieves and depravity.
